principles.text: There are four growth engines: paid, virality, content and sales. Pick one and become best in the world at it in your market.
Retention is the clearest PMF signal: if your cohort retention curve flattens above zero, some segment wants your product.
Early-customer tactics don't scale, and that's why they work. Start with the highest-trust channels, like your network, then move outward.
Start a marketplace small: constrain by geography or category, and build supply first, mostly through direct sales.
Growth comes from publishing valuable work consistently. Spend nearly all your time on the content; word of mouth beats paid channels.

sampleQA.question: How do I know if I have product-market fit?

answer.text: Track retention by cohort. If the curve flattens out and doesn't drop to zero, you have PMF with some segment of the market.
Ask users how they'd feel if the product disappeared. Over 40% answering 'very disappointed' signals PMF.
Before you have a product, try to get people to pay now, even with an invoice for early access.
Expect it to take time: about half of 25 iconic companies took months or years of iteration, and PMF isn't a one-time moment.

sampleQA.question: Where should I look for my first users?

answer.text: Consumer startups use seven reliable channels. Pick two or three; most get nearly all early growth from one or two.
The highest-ROI move is to find where your super-specific audience already gathers and give real value there, not spam.
In B2B, almost every company both taps its personal network and goes where customers spend time. Press is rarely how it starts.

sampleQA.question: Should I build growth on paid ads?

answer.text: Only if users pay you immediately so revenue funds more ads, and your product isn't something people already search for.
Don't confuse one-off turbo boosts like PR with a self-sustaining engine; invest in the engine itself.
For his own newsletter, Twitter, Facebook and LinkedIn ads were a blip compared to word-of-mouth growth.
